title: Prefix cache temperature sweep — standup notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick capture from the May 12 lab + followup standup. We ran a controlled sweep to understand how prefix cache hit-rate, small-batch heat, and kernel selection interact at varying request mix temperatures. This is an exploratory run — notes are intentionally noisy.

Attendees:
- Riley Chen (owner)
- Aisha Patel (bench harness + infra)
- Marcus Green (kernel/runtime)
- Leah Ortiz (observability + dashboards)

Agenda:
1) Recap of runs from Friday: odd p99 spikes when cache hit between 60–75%
2) Sweep design review: hit-rate targets, batch size matrix, seq-length buckets
3) Execute runs and collect trace + perf counters
4) Quick triage and action assignment

Experiment matrix (short):
- Prefix cache hit rates: 25%, 50%, 75%, 90% (simulated via synthetic workload with warmup prefixes)
- Batch sizes: 1, 4, 16 (continuous batching enabled)
- Seq-length buckets: short (32), medium (256), long (1024)
- Kernel variants: default, low-memory-quant, aten-optimized (from Marcus's branch)
- Run time: 15 minutes per cell, with 5-minute warmup

High-level observations (numbers are median across repetitions unless noted):
- Short sequences (32):
  - Batch=1: p50=6ms, p95=18ms, p99=38ms at 90% cache-hit. At 50% hit p99 jumped to ~120ms in two runs (see trace A).
  - Batch=16: throughput improved x3 as expected; p99 stable when cache-hit >=75%; below that we saw queueing-induced latency skew.
- Medium sequences (256):
  - At cache-hit 75% with aten-optimized kernel: p95 improved by ~12% vs default; p99 tail still sensitive to sudden miss bursts.
  - Low-memory-quant kernel reduced average latency slightly but increased variance for misses (p99 up ~20ms).
- Long sequences (1024):
  - Overall throughput limited by compute; cache helps but batching is primary lever. Batching=4 gave best throughput/latency tradeoff for long seqs in this infra.

Notable anomalies and traces:
- Trace A (p99 spike at short seq/batch=1/50% hit): root cause seems to be a transient KV cache eviction where multiple concurrent requests attempted to rehydrate the same prefix, causing a mini stampede and kernel recompile fallback. Marcus has the trace (trace id: trace-20250512-A) and will correlate with eviction logs.
- Memory pressure in one run (host-07): observed OOM-killer activity in the OS for a sidecar process that manages metrics exporting — unrelated to inference but amplified tail. Leah flagged host-07 and isolated it post-run.

Hypotheses:
1) Partial cache-hit regimes (40–70%) cause contention when many requests miss on hot prefixes; we should add a singleflight-like suppression for rehydrates to avoid stampedes.
2) Kernel selection fallback during recompile increases latency when multiple misses hit simultaneously; pre-warming aten-optimized for medium sequences reduces p95 but not p99.
3) Continuous batching policy needs to bias slightly towards smaller max-batch for short-seq latency-sensitive traffic to avoid queueing when cache-hit drops.

Quick follow-ups / action items:
- INF-1832 (Riley): add singleflight suppression for prefix rehydrates in the cache client; prototype branch to bench by EOD May 16.
- Marcus (PR followup): instrument kernel-compile path with a debug flag and push small telemetry in PR #2487 so we can correlate compile events to tail spikes — ETA May 15.
- Leah (dashboards): add a per-prefix rehydrate counter and host-level sidecar health panel. Put a quick alert for sidecar OOMs. ETA May 14.
- Aisha (bench harness): re-run the 50–75% hit matrix with singleflight stubbed to confirm stampede mitigation effect. Schedule for May 18.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- We should augment the synthetic workload to randomly cluster misses on the same prefix (to more closely reproduce stampede).
- Consider a lightweight LRU window that delays eviction for prefixes with >N recent reads to reduce oscillation.
- Revisit continuous-batch tunables; maybe add an adaptive policy that drops max_batch for inferred low-latency customers.

Questions to discuss next sync:
- Is singleflight suppression acceptable given memory/complexity cost? (tradeoff doc link in Confluence stubbed)
- Do we want kernel pre-warm for aten-optimized for medium sequence workloads on tiered hosts? Cost vs benefit?

Appendix: raw numbers (selected cells)
- short seq, batch=1:
  - 90% hit: qps=320, p50=6ms, p95=18ms, p99=38ms
  - 50% hit: qps=290, p50=8ms, p95=45ms, p99=118ms (2x spikes observed)
- medium seq, batch=4, aten-opt:
  - 75% hit: qps=85, p50=28ms, p95=62ms, p99=94ms
- long seq, batch=4, default kernel:
  - 90% hit: qps=18, p50=220ms, p95=480ms, p99=920ms

Links and artifacts (again):
- INF-1832: ticket for singleflight cache suppression (owner: Riley)
- PR #2487: Marcus's aten-optimized kernel branch (contains compile telemetry)
- trace-20250512-A: distributed trace in our trace store (Marcus/Leah)

Final thoughts:
This run was useful: we reproduced the p99 spike and have a concrete mitigation to try (singleflight). The run also reminded us that infra-side non-inference processes (sidecar OOM) can amplify tail and must be part of the test harness. Next run will be focused and tighter (short sequence, batch 1–4, with singleflight toggled and compile telemetry enabled).

-- Riley
